title: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues (Hornbill)
tagline: A. R. Williams on the CT scan of Tutankhamun’s mummy: what modern science can read in a three-thousand-year-old body.

overview.intro: The saga of the young king has been retold by every generation that examined his body, and the chapter’s argument is that each generation reads the mummy with the tools and the questions of its own time. The unit follows the story from Howard Carter’s forced handling of the mummy through the debates about Tutankhamun’s death to the CT scan of 2005, and asks what kind of answer a scan can give — and why the chapter ends with a question rather than a verdict.

blocks.text: The chapter opens not with discovery but with mishandling. When Howard Carter came to remove the mummy from its coffin, the resins used in burial had hardened and glued the body to the interior, and his attempts to free it resulted in damage — the mask had to be separated and the body was harmed in the process. The account uses this to establish a theme that governs the rest: every examination of the body is also an intervention in it, and the tools of one generation become the damage the next generation regrets.

Around that incident the chapter lays out the historical background a reader needs: Tutankhamun’s place in the eighteenth dynasty, the religious upheaval associated with his father’s monotheistic turn and the restoration of the god Amun that Tut’s name embodies, and the wealth of the tomb that made him famous rather than his reign. The purpose of the background is to explain why the king attracts such attention: he is the best-preserved evidence of a formative period, and his early death is an unsolved problem that each generation has tried to close.

blocks.text: Three broad explanations have been proposed over the decades, and the chapter is careful to keep them apart. Murder was the earliest popular theory: a blow to the back of the skull, found in earlier examinations, suggested a killer, and a fracture of a rib in one early reading supported it. Accident was the rival explanation, with a fall or a chariot injury proposed to account for damage to the body. A third family of explanations is medical — illness, including the genetic problems sometimes inferred from the family’s inbreeding, and infection following injury. Each theory fits some observations and not others, and each was argued from evidence that later work would reinterpret.

blocks.text: The reason the theories proliferate is methodological: each generation read the mummy with the best instrument it had, and the instrument determined the question. X-rays showed bone and shadow; later imaging could distinguish soft tissue and reconstruct the body in three dimensions. The chapter’s interest in the debate is therefore not gossipy but epistemological — what counts as evidence about a three-thousand-year-old death, and how much certainty a picture can carry.

In 2005 the mummy was taken for a computed tomography scan, which produced around seventeen hundred images that could be assembled into a three-dimensional reconstruction. The advantages over earlier radiography were decisive: instead of a few flat films the team now had a stack of slices through the whole body, which could be examined from any angle, measured precisely, and reviewed repeatedly without further handling of the mummy. The scan is non-invasive in a way that Carter’s chisels were not, which the chapter presents as the moral as well as the technical advance.

What the scan established was negative before it was positive: there was no evidence of a blow to the back of the head, which undermined the murder theory that had circulated for decades, and a fracture of the left leg was identified, with the possibilities that it occurred in life, in an accident, or even during embalming. The chapter is explicit that the evidence did not settle the cause of death, and it closes on that openness rather than on a verdict. The restraint is the point: a scan can tell you what is there, and death is an event rather than a structure, so the answer must be inferred from what the scan excludes as much as from what it shows.

learn.title: The theme: science answers its own age’s questions

blocks.text: The chapter’s title points at its argument: the saga continues because every generation reopens it. Carter wanted the treasures and damaged the body pursuing them; early twentieth-century readers wanted a murder and found skull damage; late twentieth-century medicine wanted disease and looked for pathology; the 2005 team wanted precision and non-invasive measurement, and produced images that supported none of the earlier certainties. Each answer was honest given the instrument available, and each was superseded.

That is a defensible account of how science works, and the chapter does not sneer at the earlier attempts. What it suggests is that the mummy is a text that each age reads with its own alphabet, and that the responsible position — which the chapter models — is to state what the evidence shows, to list what it excludes, and to decline to close a question that remains open. For examination answers, this theme should be tied to specific stages of the story rather than asserted abstractly: name Carter, the murder theory, and the scan, and show what each could and could not answer.

questions.prompt: State four findings or advantages of the 2005 CT scan.
questions.answer: Four points are: it produced around seventeen hundred images that could be assembled into a three-dimensional reconstruction of the body; it was non-invasive, so the mummy could be examined repeatedly without the damage that Carter’s handling caused; it found no evidence of a blow to the back of the head, which undermined the long-standing murder theory; and it identified a fracture of the left leg, for which several causes remain possible. Precise measurement from any angle is also accepted.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate what the scan found from what it made possible.

questions.prompt: Explain why the chapter ends without a verdict on the cause of death.
questions.answer: The scan answers questions about structure rather than about events. It can show bone, fractures and their positions, and it can exclude specific claims — such as a blow to the head — but a cause of death is an event in a life, and illness often leaves no visible evidence in tissue. The fracture that was found could have occurred in life, in an accident, or even during embalming, and the image alone cannot fix its timing. The chapter therefore reports what the scan established, lists what it ruled out, and declines to close a question that remains open, which is also the position responsible science takes when the evidence supports several readings. To supply a verdict at the end would be to repeat the error of earlier generations who read their own questions into the body.
questions.explanation: Three reasons are required: the distinction between structure and event, the ambiguity of the fracture found, and the methodological point about earlier generations.

questions.prompt: Trace the history of examinations of Tutankhamun’s mummy and what each could establish.
questions.answer: The history begins with physical intervention. When Howard Carter came to remove the mummy from its coffin, burial resins had hardened and attached the body to the interior, and the attempt to free it caused damage — the episode the chapter uses to establish that examining the body is also altering it. What that generation established was the contents of the tomb and the grandeur of the burial, not the circumstances of the king’s death; the treasures answered a question about wealth while the handling created a problem for everyone who came after. The middle phase is the era of the murder theory, supported by readings of damage to the skull and, in some accounts, a fractured rib: an interpretation that fitted the appetite of an age for a dramatic explanation and that rested on the limited imaging then available. The 2005 CT scan represents the third phase, and its advantages were technical and ethical at once: about seventeen hundred images assembled into a three-dimensional model, examination from any angle without touching the body, and measurements precise enough to test earlier claims. Its findings were that there was no blow to the back of the head — which dismantled the murder theory — and that a fracture of the left leg existed whose timing could not be fixed, since it might have occurred in life, in an accident or during embalming. The scan therefore excluded a celebrated explanation without replacing it with another, and the chapter closes accordingly. The pattern across the three phases is the argument of the chapter itself: each generation brought an instrument and a question, and got the answer its instrument could give.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all three phases with what each established and what it could not, and the pattern drawn out at the end.

questions.prompt: “Science answers the questions of its own age.” Discuss with reference to the chapter.
questions.answer: The claim fits the chapter’s structure closely, because each phase of the story is defined by its instrument as much as by its subject. Carter’s generation asked where the treasure was and what the burial contained, and the chisel and the brush answered; in pursuing that question it damaged the body, creating a consequence the next generation had to accommodate. The generation that wanted a murder found skull damage that could be read as a blow, and for decades the theory circulated because the evidence available — radiographs read in two dimensions — could neither confirm nor exclude it comfortably. The generation that looked for disease inferred pathology from the family’s history, and its answers were constrained by what soft-tissue imaging could then show. The 2005 team asked a different question — what does the body look like in precise, non-invasive detail — and computed tomography supplied about seventeen hundred images from which the old claim of a blow to the head could be excluded and a leg fracture identified. Each answer was genuine given its method, and each was superseded, which is exactly what the claim predicts. The counter-argument deserves weight, however: instruments do not invent their findings. The scan’s negative result about the skull is a fact about the mummy, not about the scanner, and earlier theories that failed were refuted by better evidence rather than merely abandoned with fashion. Similarly, some questions — the number of coffins, the objects in the tomb, the inscription on a cartouche — were settled permanently and not revisited, which shows that the saga continues only where the evidence genuinely underdetermines the answer. The balanced judgement is therefore that the claim is right about open questions and wrong about closed ones: where a question admits of several answers consistent with available evidence, each generation’s instrument selects among them, and the death of a king three millennia old is precisely such a question. The chapter models the honest response, which is to state what the evidence shows, name what it excludes, and leave the question open — the one position that does not age with the instrument.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the three phases tied to their instruments, the counter-argument that some findings are instrument-independent, and a judgement distinguishing open from closed questions.
